title.en: State the precondition that makes a greedy result final

summary: Show relaxation as the update mechanism and the nonnegative-weight precondition that lets settled distances stay final.
objective: Prevent a weighted shortest-path scene from producing confidently wrong answers on inputs outside its assumptions.
applies_when: A weighted shortest-path algorithm is visualised or used for routing.
Edge weights are editable by the viewer.
Distances are displayed as final once a node is settled.
example_prompts: Show Dijkstra relaxing edges with the priority queue visible.
Let me change weights and see the tree update.
negative_signals: Unweighted searches, where a queue-based traversal suffices.
Graphs with negative weights, which require a different algorithm.
not_for: Unweighted searches, where a queue-based traversal suffices.
Graphs with negative weights, which require a different algorithm.

principles: Relaxation is the whole mechanism: it tests whether the best known route to a vertex improves by going through another vertex, and updates the record if so. Showing it makes the algorithm comprehensible.

The algorithm solves the single-source shortest-path problem in edge-weighted digraphs with nonnegative weights, repeatedly adding the non-tree vertex with the lowest known distance. The nonnegative condition is what makes that greedy choice safe.
Allowing a negative weight without changing the algorithm produces answers that look authoritative and are wrong, which is worse than refusing the input.
The priority queue is the state that explains the order, so hiding it removes the reason one vertex was chosen before another.
implementation: Validate weights on input and refuse or switch algorithms when a negative weight appears, with an explanation rather than a silent result.
Visualise each relaxation as an event: the edge tested, the old distance and the new one, so improvement is legible.
Show the priority queue ordering next to the graph, and mark settled vertices distinctly from tentative ones.
Keep the shortest-path tree as explicit predecessor data so the displayed path is derived rather than drawn separately.
Recompute on weight edits rather than patching, and show which distances changed.
observable_checks: Introduce a negative weight and confirm the scene refuses or switches rather than reporting a distance.
Confirm a settled vertex distance never decreases afterwards during a run.
Compare a reported path cost against the sum of its edge weights.
Increase a weight on the current best path and confirm the tree updates coherently.

creative_affordances: The metaphor for cost, from terrain height to time to fuel, is free as long as the units are stated.
Showing the failed relaxations as well as the successful ones is often the most instructive presentation.
known_limits: Authored guidance citing the relaxation definition and the nonnegative-weight condition; negative-weight algorithms are outside it.
No runtime implementation has been benchmarked or verified for this record.

claims.statement: Relaxing an edge tests whether the best known path to its destination improves by going through its source and updates the record if so, and Dijkstra algorithm solves the single-source shortest-paths problem in edge-weighted digraphs with nonnegative weights by repeatedly relaxing and adding to the tree the non-tree vertex with the lowest known distance.
claims.scope: Weighted shortest paths with nonnegative edge weights; graphs with negative weights require different algorithms.

source_refs.locator: Relaxation; Dijkstra algorithm and the nonnegative weight condition
